Important Protocol Deviations 116 117 As noted above, in this guidance an important protocol deviation is a subset of protocol 118 deviations that might significantly affect the completeness, accuracy, and/or reliability of the 119 study data or that might significantly affect a subject’s rights, safety, or well-being. While other 120 terms such as major, critical, and significant have sometimes been used to classify such protocol 121 deviations, FDA recommends using important to encompass all these terms. 122 123 Thoughtful protocol design can help to minimize important protocol deviations. In general, 124 deviations that are classified as important should be those that could affect critical-to-quality 125 factors9 for the trial; protocol deviations related to critical-to-quality elements should be 126 identified. The quality by design approach to clinical research involves focusing on these 127 critical-to-quality factors to ensure the protection of the rights, safety, and well-being of study 128 participants; the generation of reliable and meaningful results; and the management of risks to 129 those factors using a risk-proportionate approach.10 Examples of critical-to-quality factors are 130 procedures and processes that affect the protection of trial participants and/or the efficacy or 131 safety analyses (e.g., accuracy in certain eligibility criteria, accuracy in the assessment of 132 randomization integrity, accurate collection of specific endpoint procedures). These quality 133 factors are critical to the reliability and interpretability of the study data. 134 135 It may be helpful for a protocol to define important protocol deviations and provide examples of 136 what constitutes such for the particular study. The following is a non-exhaustive list of protocol 137 deviations considered to be important by FDA due to the impact on the protection of trial 138 participants and the assessment of safety: 139 140 • Failure to conduct study procedures designed to assess participant safety or failure to 141 adequately monitor participants; for example, (1) failure to collect important laboratory 142 assessments for monitoring safety issues or (2) failure to administer the study product 143 according to specifications in the protocol 144 145 • Administration of concomitant treatment prohibited by the study protocol that may 146 increase risks to participants (e.g., drug-drug interactions) and/or impact interpretation of 147 a device’s safety and efficacy 148 149 9 See the ICH guidance for industry E8(R1) General Considerations for Clinical Studies (April 2022). Critical-to- quality factors are attributes of a study whose integrity is fundamental to the protection of study participants, the reliability and interpretability of the study results, and the decisions made based on the study results. 10 Ibid.

The use of 37 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 38 not required. 39 40 41 II. BACKGROUND 42 43 Protocol deviations are generally unintentional departures from the IRB-approved protocol and 44 are commonly not discovered until after they occur (e.g., an investigator’s failure to perform a 45 protocol-required test is discovered by the study monitor during a routine monitoring visit). 46 Protocol deviations may also include an intentional departure from the IRB-approved protocol 47 for a single participant (e.g., investigator seeks and receives sponsor and IRB approval to enroll a 48 participant above the maximum age criteria); such intentional departures should be rare because 49 the protocol should include appropriate flexibility regarding trial conduct (e.g., eligibility 50 criteria, reasonable visit windows). In the conduct of a clinical investigation, however, some 51 deviations from the specifics outlined in the protocol may occur. In 2013, FDA issued the 52 International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guidance for industry E3 Structure and Content 53 of Clinical Study Reports: Questions and Answers (R1), which includes clarifications for 54 implementing the recommendations in the ICH guidance for industry E3 Structure and Content 55 of Clinical Study Reports (July 1996) regarding the structure and content of a clinical study 56 report. To help clarify recommendations regarding the reporting of protocol deviations as 57 recommended in ICH E3, ICH E3(R1) defines a protocol deviation as “any change, divergence, 58 or departure from the study design or procedures defined in the protocol” and defines important 59 protocol deviations as “a subset of protocol deviations that might significantly affect the 60 completeness, accuracy, and/or reliability of the study data or that might significantly affect a 61 subject’s rights, safety, or well-being.”5 In this guidance, FDA is adopting the ICH E3(R1) 62 definitions of protocol deviation and important protocol deviation. 63 64 Since publication of ICH E3(R1), FDA has received feedback from interested parties requesting 65 additional guidance on reporting protocol deviations. Therefore, FDA is issuing this guidance to 66 help clarify sponsor and investigator responsibilities for identifying, mitigating, and reporting 67 protocol deviations and to provide recommendations to IRBs for evaluating protocol deviations. 68 69 Clinical investigation protocols document the study design, objectives, population, planned 70 procedures, investigational product management, method(s) of data capture, monitoring and 71 oversight plans, and statistical analysis plans either directly or by reference to associated 72 investigational plans. Protocols are a critical part of a clinical investigation, and it is essential 73 that a complete protocol is available before study initiation. 74 75 5 See Q7 in the ICH guidance for industry E3 Structure and Content of Clinical Study Reports: Questions and Answers (R1) (January 2013). The IRB should review important protocol deviations submitted by 353 investigators as soon as possible to determine any impact on participant safety or study conduct. 354 All other protocol deviations that are not classified as important and do not present an apparent 355 immediate hazard to participants do not need to be immediately reported to the IRB. 356 357 C. Protocol Amendments and Changes to an Investigational Plan 358 359 Changes in a protocol are typically not implemented before review and approval by the IRB and, 360 in some cases, by FDA. Any modifications to protocol-specified procedures that occur without 361 prior IRB approval and submission to FDA of the protocol amendment implementing the 362 modification are considered protocol deviations. Sponsors and clinical investigators are 363 encouraged to engage with IRBs as early as possible when urgent or emergent changes to the 364 protocol or informed consent are anticipated. However, when changes to the protocol or 365 investigational plan are required to minimize or eliminate immediate hazards (e.g., rapidly 366 managing an evolving situation) or to protect the life and well-being of research participants, 367 they may be implemented without prior IRB approval or before filing an amendment to the IND 368 under 21 CFR 312.30(b)(2)(ii). A change to the protocol or investigational plan that is required 369 to minimize or eliminate immediate hazards is still considered a protocol deviation if it occurs 370 before IRB approval and should be reported as such (for additional information, see section 371 III.B). For devices, certain protocol changes or modifications to the investigational plan can be 372 made without prior FDA approval.25 For example, a change or modification to the clinical 373 protocol may be reported in a 5-day notice if the changes do not affect (1) the validity of the data 374 or information resulting from the completion of the approved protocol or the relationship of 375 likely patient risk to benefit relied upon to approve the protocol; (2) the scientific soundness of 376 the investigational plan; or (3) the rights, safety, or welfare of the human subjects involved in the 377 investigation.
